official_name: Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions
plain_title: When stress or behaviour makes a physical illness worse
one_liner: A diagnosis used when psychological or behavioural factors clearly worsen a medical condition or interfere with its treatment.
in_simple_words: This diagnosis isn't about a mental illness. It's for when stress, emotions, beliefs, or behaviours are clearly making a medical condition worse or getting in the way of treating it: anxiety that triggers asthma attacks, denial that delays cancer treatment, stress that drives up blood pressure, or distress that stops someone managing diabetes. Naming it helps the medical team address the psychological side as part of care, rather than treating body and mind separately.
what_it_can_feel_like: My asthma is fine until I'm stressed. Then it's A&E. The respiratory nurse was the one who suggested I see a psychologist.
I ignored the lump for a year because I couldn't face it. The diagnosis of 'psychological factors' on my notes stung, but it got me help.
Managing diabetes with depression was impossible. Treating the depression made the diabetes manageable.
common_signs: A medical condition that's clearly worsened by stress, mood, beliefs, or behaviours
Psychological factors delaying recovery or interfering with treatment
Patterns like denial, poor adherence, or stress-triggered flares
The factor goes beyond what's expected and poses a health risk
Not better explained by another mental disorder

myths_vs_facts.myth: This diagnosis means the illness is psychological.
myths_vs_facts.fact: The illness is physical. The diagnosis flags that psychological factors are affecting it, so both can be treated.

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's a way of blaming the patient.
myths_vs_facts.fact: It's a way of getting psychological support included in medical care. The aim is help, not blame.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Stress can't really affect physical disease.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Stress and mood affect the immune system, blood pressure, pain, and health behaviours. The evidence is strong.

how_common.plain: This diagnosis is used across many medical settings; its frequency depends on the illness. Depression and anxiety are common in people with long-term physical conditions.
how_common.figure: No single prevalence figure; around 30% of people with long-term physical conditions have a co-occurring mental health condition (NHS estimates)

what_helps.plain_summary: Treatment is integrated: the medical team and a psychologist or therapist work together. CBT, stress management, and motivational approaches help with adherence and stress-triggered flares. Treating depression or anxiety, with any medication prescribed and monitored by a doctor, often improves the physical condition. Health psychologists specialize in exactly this. Peer support from others with the same illness helps people cope.
evidence_based_options: CBT and stress-management approaches adapted to the medical condition
Treatment of depression or anxiety, integrated with medical care
Health psychology or liaison psychiatry input
self_help_that_supports_care: Noticing what stresses tend to come before flares
Telling your medical team about mood and stress, not just symptoms
Peer groups for your medical condition
Small, steady habits for medication and appointments

when_to_reach_out: If stress, mood, or avoidance are making a physical illness worse or harder to manage, tell your medical team and ask about psychological support alongside treatment. It's a normal part of good care.
is_not: Having a mental illness alongside a medical condition is coded as both, not as this. Somatic symptom disorder is about distress over symptoms; this is about factors affecting an established illness.
hope_note: Treating the psychological side of a physical illness often brings the biggest improvement people have seen in years.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.
